title: Can you train economy?
goal: Judge which methods improve economy and how strong the evidence is for each: strength and plyometric training, years of endurance training, altitude and heat.

steps.title: Strength training: the best-supported tool
steps.text:
Adding strength work to running is the best-studied way to improve economy. A [meta-analysis](g:meta-analysis) of 16 studies found it lowered the oxygen cost of running by about 4% on average. Explosive training such as [plyometrics](g:plyometrics) and heavy lifting gave similar gains, isometric holds gave no clear gain, and longer programmes did better [[c:denadai]]. In five controlled trials of highly trained runners, the pooled [effect size](g:effect-size) was large [[c:balsa]].

How? Suggested reasons include stiffer muscle-tendon units and later use of less efficient fast fibres. For cycling, a review recommends heavy strength training to improve cycling economy [[c:ronnestad]].

claims.text: Across 16 studies, adding strength training lowered the oxygen cost of running by about 4%; explosive and heavy training gave similar gains, isometric training no clear gain.

evidence.quote: The concurrent training program had a small beneficial effect on RE (% change = -3.93 ± 1.19 %; p < 0.001).

In addition, explosive (% change = -4.83 ± 1.53; p < 0.001) and heavy weight (% change = -3.65 ± 2.74; p = 0.009) training programs produced similar improvements in RE, while isometric training (% change = -2.20 ± 4.37; p = 0.324) in selected studies did not induce a significant effect.

claims.text: In five controlled trials of 93 high-level middle- and long-distance runners, strength training had a large beneficial effect on running economy.

evidence.quote: The meta-analyzed effect of strength training programs on RE in high-level middle- and long-distance runners showed a large, beneficial effect (standardized mean difference [95% confidence interval] = -1.42 [-2.23 to -0.60]).

claims.text: Heavy or explosive strength training improves running economy; heavy strength training is recommended for cycling economy. Proposed mechanisms include delayed recruitment of less efficient type II fibres and stiffer muscle-tendon units.

evidence.quote: Running economy is improved by performing combined endurance training with either heavy or explosive strength training. However, heavy strength training is recommended for improving cycling economy.

It is suggested that the improved endurance performance may relate to delayed activation of less efficient type II fibers, improved neuromuscular efficiency, conversion of fast-twitch type IIX fibers into more fatigue-resistant type IIA fibers, or improved musculo-tendinous stiffness.

steps.title: Heavy or plyometric?
steps.text:
Which method works best is still argued. A 2022 meta-analysis of 22 studies found a small gain from heavy lifting and only a trivial one from plyometrics; near-maximal loads (90% or more of [one-rep max](g:one-rep-max)) and longer programmes (10–14 weeks) did best [[c:eihara]].

A 2024 meta-analysis, with moderate-certainty evidence, found that heavy loads helped across speeds, more so at high speeds and in runners with a high VO₂max. Plyometrics helped at slow speeds (12 km·h⁻¹ or less). Moderate loads and isometric work showed no clear gain [[c:llanos]].

A fair reading: heavy, near-maximal lifting for 10 weeks or more is the safest bet for trained runners.

claims.text: Heavy resistance training gave a small improvement in running economy, larger than the trivial one from plyometric training; near-maximal loads gave larger effects.

evidence.quote: The pooled effect size for running economy in heavy resistance training was greater (g = - 0.32 [95% confidence intervals [CIs] - 0.55 to - 0.10]: effect size = small) than that in plyometric training (g = -0.13 [95% CIs - 0.47 to 0.21]: trivial).

Heavy resistance training with nearly maximal loads (≥ 90% of 1 repetition maximum [1RM], g = - 0.31 [95% CIs - 0.61 to - 0.02]: small) provided greater effects than those with lower loads (< 90% 1RM, g = - 0.17 [95% CIs - 1.05 to 0.70]: trivial).

claims.text: With moderate-certainty evidence, high-load strength training improved running economy (more at high speeds and high VO₂max), plyometrics improved it at speeds of 12 km·h⁻¹ or less, and submaximal-load and isometric training showed no clear gain.

evidence.quote: The certainty of the evidence was found to be moderate for high load training, submaximal load training, plyometric training and isometric training methods and low for combined methods.
Plyometric training improved running economy at speeds ≤ 12.00 km/h (small effect, ES = - 0.307, p = 0.028, β1 = 0.470, p = 0.017).
high load strength training might be particularly effective in improving running economy (i) in athletes with a high VO2max, and (ii) at high running speeds.

debate.question: Is plyometric training as good as heavy lifting for running economy?

sides.position: About equal: explosive and heavy strength training gave similar gains in running economy.

Heavy lifting has the edge: in one meta-analysis plyometrics gave only a trivial pooled gain; in another they helped mainly at slow speeds (12 km·h⁻¹ or less), while heavy loads helped more at high speeds.

steps.title: Years, not weeks
steps.text:
Most trials last 6–14 weeks, but economy seems to keep improving over years of training. The best-known case: Paula Radcliffe's running economy improved by about 15% between 1992 and 2003, as she became the marathon world record holder [[c:radcliffe]].

That is one athlete, measured over a decade in which age, body mass, shoes and lab methods may all have changed: it shows what is possible, not what to expect.

The meta-analyses point the same way on a smaller scale: longer strength programmes gave bigger gains, and the largest improvements seem to need long-term training [[c:denadai-long]]. In cycling, GE rose and fell with a season's training, as the cycling lesson showed.

claims.text: The women's marathon world record holder improved her running economy by about 15% between 1992 and 2003.

evidence.quote: PR's data demonstrate a 15% improvement in running economy between 1992 and 2003 suggesting that improvements in this parameter are very important in allowing a distance runner to continue to improve their performance over the longer-term.

claims.text: Longer strength-training programmes gave larger improvements in running economy; long-term programmes seem necessary for the largest gains.

evidence.quote: This model showed that the magnitude of the % change in RE was larger for longer training duration (β = -0.83 ± 0.72, p = 0.02).
However, long-term training programs seem to be necessary when the largest possible improvement in RE is desired.
In addition, running economy appears to be improved better when training is performed for a longer period in both heavy resistance and plyometric training.

steps.title: Altitude: a small, contested gain
steps.text:
In [live high–train low](g:live-high-train-low) (LHTL), athletes sleep at real or simulated altitude and train near sea level. In 22 elite runners split into three groups, submaximal VO₂ after 20 days of LHTL was 3.3% lower than in the other two groups, with no change in [haemoglobin mass](g:haemoglobin-mass), RER or lactate [[c:saund04]]. A later study (about 46 nights, 18 runners) found a similar 3.2% fall, this time with a rise in haemoglobin mass [[c:saund09]].

But these are small studies from one research group, and an independent review judged the case for recommending altitude training to be weak [[c:lundby]]. A 3% change is also within the 1.3–5% that economy varies from test to test in the same runner [[c:re-te]].

claims.text: After 20 days of live high–train low at simulated altitude, elite runners' submaximal VO₂ was 3.3% lower than in control groups, with no change in RER, heart rate or haemoglobin mass and no rise in blood lactate.

evidence.quote: Vo(2) (l/min) averaged across the three submaximal running speeds was 3.3% lower (P = 0.005) after LHTL compared with either LMTM or LLTL.
Ve, respiratory exchange ratio, heart rate, and Hb(mass) were not significantly different after the three interventions.

There was no evidence of an increase in lactate concentration after the LHTL intervention, suggesting that the lower aerobic cost of running was not attributable to an increased anaerobic energy contribution.

claims.text: In nine elite middle-distance runners, about 46 nights of live high–train low lowered submaximal VO₂ by 3.2% compared with nine controls, and raised haemoglobin mass by 4.9%.

evidence.quote: ALT decreased submaximal V(O)(2) (Lmin(-1)) (-3.2%, 90% confidence intervals, -1.0% to -5.2%, p=0.02)
increased Hb(mass) (4.9%, 2.3-7.6%, p=0.01)

claims.text: A review concluded that the foundation for recommending altitude training to athletes is weak.

evidence.quote: Based on the available literature, the foundation to recommend altitude training to athletes is weak.

claims.text: In well-controlled studies, running economy varies by 1.3–5% within the same runner between tests.

evidence.quote: intraindividual variation in RE between 1.3% and 5% at speeds between 12 and 18 km

debate.question: Does altitude training improve running economy?

sides.position: Yes: live high–train low lowered submaximal VO₂ by about 3% in elite runners, in two controlled studies.
Not established: the evidence for altitude training's benefits is weak, and a 3% change is close to test-to-test noise.

steps.title: Heat: a performance aid, not an economy aid
steps.text:
[Heat acclimation](g:heat-acclimation) can clearly help performance. In 12 trained cyclists, 10 days of training in 40 °C heat raised VO₂max by 5% and time-trial performance by 6% even in cool conditions, alongside a 6.5% rise in [plasma volume](g:plasma-volume) and a higher maximal [cardiac output](g:cardiac-output) [[c:lorenzo]].

But economy isn't the route. In runners after 5 days of heat training, running economy got worse, in the heat-trained and control groups alike [[c:james]]. And a hot day itself lowers cycling GE by about a point [[c:hettinga-heat]].

Grading the methods for economy: strength training, moderate; altitude, weak and contested; heat, no support so far.

claims.text: In 12 trained cyclists, 10 days of heat acclimation raised VO₂max by 5% and time-trial performance by 6% in cool conditions, with a 6.5% rise in plasma volume and a higher maximal cardiac output.

evidence.quote: Heat acclimation increased VO2max by 5% in cool (66.8 ± 2.1 vs. 70.2 ± 2.3 ml·kg(-1)·min(-1), P = 0.004)
Heat acclimation improved time-trial performance by 6% in cool (879.8 ± 48.5 vs. 934.7 ± 50.9 kJ, P = 0.005)
Heat acclimation increased plasma volume (6.5 ± 1.5%) and maximal cardiac output in cool and hot conditions (9.1 ± 3.4% and 4.5 ± 4.6%, respectively).

claims.text: After 5 days of short-term heat acclimation or matched training in cool conditions, running economy got worse in both groups.

evidence.quote: Running economy (RE) deteriorated following both training programmes (p = 0.008).

claims.text: Gross efficiency in cycling was about 0.9 percentage points lower in the heat.

evidence.quote: GE was 0.9% lower in H compared to N (19.6+/-1.1% vs. 20.5+/-1.4%) (P<0.05).

points: Strength training lowers the oxygen cost of running by about 4% on average (moderate evidence); heavy, near-maximal lifting for 10+ weeks is the safest bet, and heavy strength work is recommended for cycling economy.
Plyometrics versus heavy lifting is debated; plyometrics seem to help mainly at slow speeds, isometric and moderate loads not clearly at all.
Economy can keep improving over years (about 15% in one world-record runner), but one case can't set expectations.
Altitude (LHTL) lowered submaximal VO₂ by about 3% in small studies from one group: weak and contested, and close to test-to-test noise.
Heat acclimation helps performance through blood volume and the heart; it has not been shown to improve economy.

variants.stem: In the 16-study meta-analysis, which kind of strength training gave no clear gain in running economy?

options.why: Right: isometric training (−2.2%, not significant) did not clearly improve economy.
Explosive training gave the largest average gain, about 4.8%.
Heavy weight training improved economy by about 3.7%.

variants.stem: A meta-analysis reports a 'large' effect of strength training on running economy (effect size −1.42, 95% CI −2.23 to −0.60), pooled from 5 trials and 93 runners. Why read it with care?

options.text: Few, small trials give an imprecise estimate: the true effect could be much smaller
options.why: Right: the wide confidence interval, from 5 small trials, means the size is uncertain even if the direction is consistent.

options.text: Effect sizes can't be negative, so the result is an error
options.why: A negative effect size here just means oxygen cost went down, which is an improvement.
Controlled trials are exactly what meta-analyses of interventions pool.

options.text: A large effect always means the trials were industry funded
options.why: Large effects can have many causes; nothing here points to funding.

variants.stem: A sub-elite 10 km runner with a VO₂max of 70 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹, who races at about 18 km·h⁻¹, adds two gym sessions a week. Which programme does the evidence favour for his economy?

options.text: Heavy lifting at near-maximal loads for 10 weeks or more
options.why: Right: high loads helped most at high speeds and high VO₂max, and near-maximal loads and longer programmes did best.

options.text: Light circuits at about 50% of 1RM for 4 weeks
options.why: Submaximal loads showed no clear gain, and short programmes did less.
Isometric training showed no clear gain in economy.
Plyometrics helped mainly at slow speeds (12 km·h⁻¹ or less), and short programmes did little.

variants.stem: A cyclist wants to add strength work to improve cycling economy. Which form does a review of running and cycling studies recommend?

options.why: Right: heavy strength training is the form recommended for cycling economy.
Explosive training is supported for running economy, but heavy strength work is recommended for cycling.
Isometric training had no clear effect even in running.
Light loads showed no clear gain in running economy, and they are not what the review recommends.

variants.stem: A runner can hold 60.0 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ in a race; her oxygen cost is 200 mL·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹, so she runs 18.0 km·h⁻¹. If strength training lowers her cost by 4%, what speed can she hold at the same VO₂?

options.why: This lowers the cost by 4 mL (to 196) instead of 4%.
A lower cost per km means more speed for the same VO₂.
This takes 4% off the speed; a cheaper km lets her go faster, not slower.

variants.solution: New cost = 200 × 0.96 = 192 mL·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹. Speed = VO₂ × 60 ÷ cost = 60.0 × 60 ÷ 192 = 18.75 km·h⁻¹.

variants.stem: A triathlete can hold 54.0 mL·kg⁻¹·min⁻¹ on the run with an oxygen cost of 216 mL·kg⁻¹·km⁻¹, so she runs 15.0 km·h⁻¹. If her cost falls by 4%, what speed can she hold at the same VO₂?

options.why: This lowers the cost by 4 mL (to 212) instead of 4%.
A lower cost per km means more speed for the same VO₂.
This takes 4% off the speed; a cheaper km lets her go faster, not slower.

variants.stem: What do meta-analyses of strength training suggest about programme length and gains in running economy?

options.why: Right: the gain grew with programme duration, and the largest gains seem to need long-term training.

options.text: The full gain comes within 2 weeks
options.why: Programmes were 4 weeks or more, and longer ones did better.

options.text: Length doesn't matter, only the load
options.why: Both load and length mattered; longer was better.
The opposite: longer programmes improved economy more.

variants.stem: A coach cites Paula Radcliffe's 15% gain in running economy over 11 years to promise his athletes similar gains. What is the best judgement?

options.text: An overreach: one exceptional athlete over a decade of changes can't set expectations
options.why: Right: a single case, with age, mass, shoes and methods changing over time, shows what is possible, not what is typical.

options.text: Sound: case studies are the strongest kind of evidence
options.why: A case study of one athlete sits near the bottom of the evidence pyramid.

options.text: Sound, as long as they train the same volume
options.why: Matching volume doesn't make one athlete's result typical.

options.text: Wrong: economy can't change after age 20
options.why: Economy does change with training at any age; the problem is generalising from one person.

variants.stem: After 20 days of live high–train low, elite runners' submaximal VO₂ fell 3.3%, with no change in haemoglobin mass, RER or blood lactate. Which explanations does this make unlikely?

options.text: More haemoglobin, a shift to carbohydrate, or more anaerobic energy
options.why: Right: haemoglobin mass and RER didn't change, and lactate didn't rise, so these can't explain the lower VO₂.

options.text: Better running mechanics after the camp
options.why: Mechanics weren't measured, so they remain a possible explanation, as do changes inside the muscle.

options.text: Changes inside the muscle, such as in the mitochondria
options.why: These remain possible: the study measured blood and fuel markers, not the muscle itself.

variants.stem: How strong is the evidence that live high–train low improves running economy?

options.text: Weak and contested: a few small studies, mostly from one group
options.why: Right: two small controlled studies found about 3% falls in submaximal VO₂, and an independent review calls the case for altitude training weak.

options.text: Strong: several large randomised trials agree
options.why: The studies are small (18–22 runners) and come mainly from one research group.

options.text: Proven, and explained by higher haemoglobin mass
options.why: In the 20-day study haemoglobin mass didn't change, so it can't explain that result; in the longer study it rose, but VO₂ fell by the same amount.
VO₂ fell, not rose, in both studies.

variants.stem: An online coach claims heat training 'makes you more economical'. Which reading fits the evidence?

options.text: It helps via blood volume and the heart; no economy gain is shown
options.why: Right: heat acclimation raised plasma volume and cardiac output, and economy didn't improve in the runners studied.

options.text: Correct: heat training lowers the oxygen cost of running by about 5%
options.why: The 5% figure is the rise in VO₂max, not a fall in oxygen cost.

options.text: Correct, because cycling gross efficiency is higher in the heat
options.why: GE is about a point lower in the heat, not higher.

options.text: Wrong: heat training has no performance benefit at all
options.why: It improved time-trial performance by 6% in cool conditions in one study.

variants.stem: A triathlete has time for one winter add-on to improve run economy: heavy strength training, a 3-week altitude tent, or heat sessions. Ranked by the strength of evidence for economy, which order is right?

options.why: Right: strength training has consistent meta-analyses; altitude a few small studies; heat no economy gain shown.
Altitude evidence is weaker and contested; strength training rests on several meta-analyses.
Heat acclimation hasn't been shown to improve economy at all.

options.text: All three are equally well supported
options.why: The evidence differs a lot: moderate for strength, weak for altitude, none so far for heat.
